scenes.tts: The reigning belief was that the molecules of life carried a vital force — that you could not build them from ordinary, lifeless matter, only borrow them from something already alive.
scenes.visual: vital-force belief: lifeless matter cannot yield molecules of life

scenes.tts: One afternoon in 1828 Wöhler heated an inorganic salt and watched urea crystallize in his flask. Urea is the nitrogen waste animals flush out through their kidneys. There was no kidney in the room.
scenes.visual: 1828: inorganic salt heated in flask, urea crystallizes, no kidney

scenes.tts: He wrote to his mentor Berzelius with a joke, not a manifesto: "I can no longer, as it were, hold back my chemical urine; and I have to let out that I can make urea without needing a kidney." The line is irreverent and exact at once.
scenes.visual: letter to Berzelius: the joke, the quote

scenes.tts: He was sharing surprise with a friend, and in the same breath dissolving the boundary the whole century had assumed. The molecules of life obey the chemistry of everything else.
scenes.visual: boundary between living and dead chemistry dissolves

scenes.tts: What he had opened he called "a primeval forest, a monstrous and boundless thicket," and claimed only the willingness to go in again. The four classes of biomolecules in this chapter are the trees in that forest.
